title: Power from the Sea

paragraphs.text: It’s been a long time coming. People first started harnessing the sea’s power at least as long ago as AD900, with water mills placed over tidal rivers to grind cereals into flour. But when the industrial revolution came along, the sea lost out to coal and oil. Now the position may be changing. Faced with the depletion of fossil fuels and concern over climate change, governments are pumping more money into exploring the sea's potential. It could even be an economic bonus for Britain. The expertise at offshore operations, which some companies have gained in exploiting the oil fields beneath the North Sea, places them in a good position to reap a potentially vast export market.

Tidal currents are caused as oceans bulge in response to the gravitational pull of the moon and sun. The continuous flow of water speeds up as it is squeezed between landmasses. But this is not the only way in which oceans carry exploitable power. There’s also the energy wrapped up in waves created by the wind blowing over the water. On a global scale, wave energy represents a massive resource, because seas cover 70 per cent of the world’s surface. Engineers are tackling the key problem of the survivability of wave energy devices that must operate at the harsh interface of sea and air. In the 1970s, an Edinburgh University professor, Stephen Salter, led efforts to exploit the resource. The ‘Salter Duck’ was a 3,000-tonne float that drove a generator with energy produced by its motion of bobbing up and down on the water. But his much-admired invention was killed off in the mid-1980s when European officials decided it was not cost-effective, although later it was found that this decision was based on a huge miscalculation.

Meanwhile, other engineers had chosen tidal currents as the most viable sea-power option. Tides have a key advantage over most other renewable energy resources: they are almost continuous and entirely predictable. The lull in the speed of an ocean current comes, however, when the tide is turning. At this point, backup power from other sources has to be fed into the national power network to meet demand.

The first river-based scheme centered on building a barrage across the river mouth to trap a head of water at high tide, letting it escape through turbines in order to drive generators. In the mid-1960s, one such scheme began operation in Brittany in northern France and still supplies most of the region’s electricity. Another has been proposed for Canada’s Bay of Fundy, which has the largest tidal range in the world. But barrages have been found to cause serious environmental problems. They prevent fish migration and ruin sensitive habitats, which are located between low and high tide lines. This isn’t the only drawback. The building of an 8,640-megawatt scheme — enough to supply electricity to more than 8 million homes in the UK — has been proposed for the Severn Estuary, which has the world’s second highest tidal range. But the plan is on the shelf, partly because the estuary route is one of the main outlets for human waste from central England and Wales. Plugging it could thus produce the world’s most disgusting body of water.

Yet the potential of sea power has continued to captivate scientists and while developments continue on a host of wave energy converters, in the last few years both government and private financiers have finally taken the plunge to back tidal energy projects. A number of different technologies are in development, but arguably the most advanced and perhaps the most elegantly straightforward, is the marine current turbine. This is essentially an underwater wind turbine — a propeller mounted on a tower. A principal advantage is that the underwater environment is calm, even when storms are raging on the surface. And as water is 800 times denser than air, these marine current turbines can capture much larger volumes of energy than wind turbines can from comparable air-flow speeds, although they must also be squat and heavy, to resist the massive loads involved. While both onshore and offshore wind turbines face huge opposition from those who see them as an eyesore, the first marine current turbine designs present minimal intrusion on the view. Crucially, too, they appear to have little impact on the environment; the blades move so slowly that marine creatures can easily move through. The international organization Greenpeace is a big supporter while, conversely, wind turbines are meeting opposition from environmentalists for harming birdlife.

Twenty years ago Stephen Salter remarked that wave energy would get off the ground the week after a major nuclear accident in the UK,’ says Professor David Elliott, Director of the Open University’s Energy and Environment Research Unit. ‘It’s still true that it just needs a big government decision to go for it and make it all happen. The resource and the technology is all there.’

subtitle: The oceans are vast, tides are regular and currents are predictable yet sea power is the least developed form of renewable energy. Clara Penn reports on how some projects are changing this situation
